title: The line between sports hero and gambling shill is fast disappearing
summary: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – rich When Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow. More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did , rather than pockets the cash to endorse them. title: The Breakdown | North v south: who makes the cut in our fantasy XVs for a hemisphere head-to-head?
summary: Before the Nations Championship finale, picking MVPs for all-star hemisphere teams plus a global XV is far from easy This week the world’s top 400 rugby players will be assembling in the same city . You can only hope London’s steak restaurants and cafes are braced for the simultaneous influx of an army of huge men with even larger appetites. If tall buildings start to sway in the Twickenham area, you will know the buildup to this weekend’s Nations Championship finals is intensifying. Which begs a timely question. Mirror, mirror on the wall, who’s the most valuable of them all? With this week billed as a north v south duel – there is even a trophy on offer to the champion hemisphere – it is not a bad moment to sit down with pen and paper and play fantasy selector.
